iDebug: Testing and Fixing Your Game

Year 6, Lesson 6

steps.label: Today's Task
steps.content:
Today's Task

Your game is built. Today you test it properly, and fix what you find.

  • Objective: develop strategies for testing and debugging your program.
  • Success criteria: find and fix errors in your program.

Key vocabulary

Test; bug; debug; amend; systematically.

steps.label: Testing Systematically
steps.content:
Testing Systematically

Programmers do not just click around and hope. They test systematically.

  • A systematic test goes through every way the program could be used, not just the ones you expect players to try.
  • Every statement in the code should be run and checked at least once.
  • Good testers deliberately try to make the game fail - clicking fast, doing things in the wrong order, trying to go off the edge of the stage - to make sure it is bug free.

items.prompt: Which of these is closest to "testing systematically"?
options: Going through every way the game could be used, on purpose, to try to find problems
Playing the game once, the normal way, and stopping if nothing looks wrong
Asking a friend if the game looks good
items.explain: Systematic testing is planned and thorough - it does not stop at the first normal playthrough.

items.prompt: Why do testers deliberately try to make a game fail?
options: To prove the programmer got it wrong
To find bugs before a player does, so they can be fixed
Because it is more fun than playing normally
items.explain: Trying to break the game on purpose is how testers find the bugs a normal playthrough would miss.

steps.label: Activity 1: Test Your Own Game
steps.content:
Activity 1: Test Your Own Game

Work independently - play your own game systematically, using your plan to check it does what it should.

  1. Open your saved project in TurboWarp using the button.
  2. Play it the normal way first, then try to break it on purpose: click fast, try the edges, do things out of order.
  3. Keep a mental note (or a scrap of paper) of anything that goes wrong - you will record it properly in Activity 2.

The Slides and TurboWarp switcher stays at the top right - use it whenever you need the next instruction.

steps.label: Describing a Bug Precisely
steps.content:
Describing a Bug Precisely

"It doesn't work" does not help anyone fix a bug. A good bug report answers three questions:

  • Where did the bug happen? What were you doing when it happened?
  • What happened? What actually went wrong?
  • What did you expect to happen? What did you think would happen instead?

You will use these three questions on the Testing Record sheet in the next activity.

steps.label: Activity 2: Swap and Record Bugs
steps.content:
Activity 2: Swap and Record Bugs

Swap places with a partner. Play their game systematically, the same way you played your own. Your own eyes get used to your own game, so a fresh player often finds bugs you missed.

For every bug you find in your partner's game, record it using the three questions from the last slide, then hand your notes back to them and discuss what you found.

items.prompt: Bug 1 - where did it happen (what were you doing)? What happened? What did you expect to happen?
items.modelAnswer: A complete answer names a specific action (for example: pressing the up arrow near the top wall), the actual result (for example: the sprite went through the wall), and the expected result (for example: the sprite should have stopped at the wall).

items.prompt: Bug 2 (if you found a second one) - where did it happen? What happened? What did you expect to happen? If you only found one bug, write "Only one bug found" here.
items.modelAnswer: Either a second specific bug report in the same three-part format, or an honest note that only one bug was found.

steps.label: Activity 3: Fix Your Own Bugs
steps.content:
Activity 3: Fix Your Own Bugs

Take back the bug reports your partner wrote about your game. Work independently to correct every bug they found.

  1. Open your project in TurboWarp using the button.
  2. For each bug report, find the block or blocks causing it and amend them.
  3. Test again after each fix - do not fix everything at once and hope, check each one on its own.

The Slides and TurboWarp switcher stays at the top right - use it whenever you need the next instruction.

Before moving on

Every bug your partner recorded about your game should now be fixed and retested.

steps.label: Easier and Harder
steps.content:
Easier and Harder

EasierAsk an adult to help you identify exactly which block is causing a bug before you try to fix it.
HarderEvaluate your partner's finished game and discuss how it could be extended or improved - do not just find bugs, suggest a genuine improvement.

steps.label: Reflecting on Testing
steps.content:
Reflecting on Testing

Look back at what actually happened today, then answer honestly - this is marked by you, not a computer.

items.prompt: Describe one bug your partner found in your game, and how you fixed it.
items.modelAnswer: A good answer names a specific bug (not just "it was broken") and a specific fix (which block was changed, and how).

items.prompt: Why is it useful to have someone else test your game, instead of only testing it yourself?
items.modelAnswer: You already know how your own game is supposed to be played, so you tend to only play it the expected way. Someone who did not write it will try things you would not think of, so they find bugs you would miss.
